lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Opening admiration for her verses; establishes the literary courtship.

lines.text: Such a letter from such a hand!
lines.note: Her awed response to his letter; shows the first spark.

lines.text: And in the meantime I have learnt to know your voice, not merely from the poetry but from the kindness in it.
lines.note: She hears his kindness in his voice, not only his poetry.

lines.text: See now, how, of that 'Friendship' you offer me (and here Juliet's word rises to my lips)--I feel sure once and for ever.
lines.note: He answers her offered friendship with certainty.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Her playful redefinition of spring; a private stylistic joke.

lines.text: I do not find it take away from my feeling of the magnanimity of Prometheus that he should, in truth, complain (as he does from beginning to end) of what he finds himself suffering.
lines.note: His reading of Prometheus; early shared Greek ground.

lines.text: Oh! the 'Flight of the Duchess'--do let us hear more of her!
lines.note: Her delight in the Duchess; a poem that becomes theirs.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: He frames love beyond any possible loss.

lines.text: And now I will dare ... yes, dearest, kiss you back to my heart again; my own.
lines.note: A tender promise to kiss her back to his heart.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: She calls his love a dream made real.

lines.text: 'Luria' is to climb to the place of a great work, I see.
lines.note: She sees Luria growing into a great work.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: He jokes that marriage would have to be invented.

lines.text: For me, I adore you.
lines.note: She says you are her one light.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first unguarded declaration of love sets the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth answers Robert's hint that he had almost seen her.

lines.text: Who told you of my sculls and spider webs--Horne?
lines.note: Robert's skulls and spider webs become a running private joke.

lines.text: Who told me of your skulls and spiders?
lines.note: Elizabeth claims she knew Robert's skulls without being told.

lines.text: Next Wednesday--if you know how happy you make me! may I not say that, my dear friend, when I feel it from my soul?
lines.note: Robert counts down to another visit and the joy it brings.

lines.text: So, till to-morrow,--my light through the dark week.
lines.note: Robert calls Elizabeth his light through the dark week.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert wraps his whole life around Elizabeth in a love letter.

lines.text: It comes at eight o'clock--the post says eight ...
lines.note: Elizabeth greets the postman's knock as the arrival of Robert's letter.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert pledges to live and die with Elizabeth's ring and hair.

lines.text: So I put the hair into his locket, which I wear habitually, and which never had hair before--the natural use of it being for perfume:--and this is the best perfume for all hours, besides the completing of a prophecy.
lines.note: Elizabeth keeps Robert's hair in a locket and completes a prophecy.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's chestnut tree and west wind from an early letter.

lines.text: Do you remember when you wrote first to me ‘May God bless you and me in that!’
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers Robert's first blessing before they met.

lines.text: Beside I got tired with the long walk from Carlyle’s last night—for I went and saw him to heart’s content—and he talked characteristically and well, and constringingly, bracingly.
lines.note: Robert returns from Carlyle with news and affection.

lines.text: Now let me kiss you—which kiss, as I am to really kiss you to-morrow, my sweetest, I shall dare tell the truth of to myself, and say ‘The real will be better.’
lines.note: Robert kisses Elizabeth in anticipation of seeing her next day.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's early open declaration that he loves her.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Elizabeth's first grateful reply to his letter.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's spring hope of finally seeing her.

lines.text: And I have the cream of it in your friendship, and a little more, and I do not envy much the milkers of the cows.
lines.note: Elizabeth calls his friendship the cream of her world.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: Robert says he loves to see her from week to week.

lines.text: I never shall forget these things, my dearest friend; nor remember them more coldly.
lines.note: Elizabeth promises she will never remember these things coldly.

lines.text: The poems ... yours ... which you left with me,--are full of various power and beauty and character, and you must let me have my own gladness from them in my own way.
lines.note: Elizabeth praises the poems' various power and beauty.

lines.text: I am not conscious of thinking or feeling but about you, with some reference to you--so I will live, so may I die!
lines.note: Robert says his whole life is wound around her.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: Elizabeth says Robert cannot guess what he is to her.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert vows to live and die with her ring and hair.

lines.text: And therefore, because you are the best, only dearest!——Robert.
lines.note: Elizabeth first speaks the name Robert.

lines.text: Altogether, then, I forgive you, Robert—and it is glorious for me to have something to forgive you for, who are the best so out of measure!—I seize the opportunity.
lines.note: Elizabeth forgives Robert and says she loves him.

lines.text: Ever dearest, your ‘Hush’ came too late.
lines.note: Elizabeth says his 'Hush' came too late after she had spoken.

lines.text: Dearest Ba, the love was as you admit, beneath all the foolish words—I will lay your pardon to my heart with the other blessings.
lines.note: Robert says his love is beneath her goodness.

lines.text: Do you know I was once not very far from seeing--really seeing you?
lines.note: Early Robert remembers almost seeing Elizabeth, the first near-meeting behind their whole story.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth answers Robert's near-miss with wonder at the almost-acquaintance, echoing his first letter.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert turns the near-miss into a promise of spring friendship and the hoped-for Chapel sight.

lines.text: Nay--I must have last word--as all people in the wrong desire to have--and then, no more of the subject.
lines.note: Robert takes the last word because he is in the wrong, acknowledging the hurt he caused Elizabeth.

lines.text: You said I had given you great pain--so long as I stop that, think anything of me you choose or can!
lines.note: Robert asks only that he stop giving Elizabeth pain, a direct apology for his wild words.

lines.text: You will think me the most changeable of all the changeable; but indeed it is not my fault that I cannot, as I wished, receive you on Wednesday.
lines.note: Elizabeth, changeable only by circumstance, postpones their meeting while still hoping to see him.

lines.text: Do tell me what you mean precisely by your 'Bells and Pomegranates' title.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks for the meaning of Robert's 'Bells and Pomegranates' title, their private literary shorthand.

lines.text: I meant the whole should prove at last.
lines.note: Robert says the whole work was meant to prove itself at last, answering Elizabeth's question.

lines.text: 'The Duchess' appears to me more than ever a new-minted golden coin--the rhythm of it answering to your own description, 'Speech half asleep, or song half awake?'
lines.note: Elizabeth praises 'The Duchess' as a new-minted golden coin, showing her close reading of his rhythm.

lines.text: Do you remember how you told me of 'Luria' last year, in one of your early letters?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's early letter about 'Luria', a callback to their first months.

lines.text: Can it be the same 'Luria,' I think, that 'golden-hearted Luria,' whom you talked of to me, when you complained of keeping 'wild company,' in the old dear letter?
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers Robert's phrase 'golden-hearted Luria' and applies it to him, not only the hero.

lines.text: You were right to bid me never again wish my poor flowers were ‘diamonds’—you could not, I think, speak so to my heart of any diamonds.
lines.note: Robert accepts Elizabeth's reproof about wishing his flowers were diamonds, turning back to her gift.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first letter already says he loves her books and her, setting the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Sympathy is dear--very dear to me: but the sympathy of a poet, and of such a poet, is the quintessence of sympathy to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth's reply values a poet's sympathy as the quintessence of sympathy, showing the bond forming.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's spring promise to see her turns the letters toward a real meeting.

lines.text: I shall be ready on Tuesday I hope, but I hate and protest against your horrible 'entomology.'
lines.note: Elizabeth's protest against his 'horrible entomology' is a private joke about how he pins her words down.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: Robert compares her criticism to tying him up like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl, a vivid private joke between them.

lines.text: It is very kind to send these flowers--too kind--why are they sent? and without one single word ... which is not too kind certainly.
lines.note: Elizabeth notices his flowers sent without a word, a concrete moment of his wordless care.

lines.text: I scarcely know how to write what is to be written nor indeed why it is to be written and to what end.
lines.note: Her overwhelmed letter before the Pisa journey shows the relationship becoming serious and painful.

lines.text: And since I wrote what is above, I have been reading among other poems that sonnet--'Past and Future'--which affects me more than any poem I ever read.
lines.note: Robert's reaction to her 'Past and Future' sonnet shows her work deeply affecting him.

lines.text: When I first saw you--I saw your eyes--since then, you, it should appear, see mine--but I only know yours are there, and have to use that memory as if one carried dried flowers about when fairly inside the garden-enclosure.
lines.note: Robert recalls first seeing her eyes, a private memory of their earliest meetings.

lines.text: Dearest, you know how to say what makes me happiest, you who never think, you say, of making me happy!
lines.note: Elizabeth says he knows how to say what makes her happiest, a clear statement of his effect on her.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth's memory of the chestnut tree and west wind recalls Robert's earlier letter.

lines.text: No, No! indeed I never did.
lines.note: Elizabeth says she never called anyone by such a name, making his name intimate and new.

lines.text: ‘Did I ever receive such a letter?’
lines.note: Elizabeth says she never received such a letter except from him, showing his unique place with her.

lines.text: At from half-past three to four, then—four will not, I suppose, be too late.
lines.note: Their final arrangements for leaving together end the long correspondence in action rather than words.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's early, unmistakable declaration that he loves her as well as her poetry.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth's wondering whether their near-miss meeting had really happened.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert turns their first contact from 'honour of acquaintance' into friendship and a spring meeting.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: A vivid spring promise that he will surely see her.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Elizabeth's private joke redefining spring in her own 'style'.

lines.text: But if my truest heart's wishes avail, as they have hitherto done, you shall laugh at East winds yet, as I do!
lines.note: Robert's callback to Elizabeth's east-wind complaint, promising she will laugh at east winds.

lines.text: You and I seem to meet in a mild contrarious harmony ... as in the 'si no, si no' of an Italian duet.
lines.note: Elizabeth's private image of their 'mild contrarious harmony' like an Italian duet.

lines.text: And I, too, love to have few friends, and to live alone, and to see you from week to week.
lines.note: Robert's quiet statement of wanting few friends and seeing her week to week.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: Robert's delight that Elizabeth likes the 'Duchess'.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's declaration that his whole life is wound around her.

lines.text: God bless and strengthen you, my ever dearest dearest—I will not trust myself to speak of my feelings for you—worship well belongs to such fortitude.
lines.note: A farewell blessing as the journey to Italy nears.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's last-moment sense that she will have him only to love her.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth's explicit question of whether this is her last letter.

lines.text: Do you pray for me to-night, Robert?
lines.note: Elizabeth's final request that he pray for her.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Your first letter declares love for her books and for her.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Her first reply thanks you from the bottom of her heart.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: You promise that spring will bring your meeting.

lines.text: Three scratches with a pen, even with this pen,--and you have the green little Syrenusa where I have sate and heard the quails sing.
lines.note: You send her an imagined Syrenusa and singing quails.

lines.text: As to the Polkas and Cellariuses I do not covet them of course ... but what a strange world you seem to have, to me at a distance--what a strange husk of a world!
lines.note: She writes from a distance about your strange London world.

lines.text: You let 'flowers be sent you in a letter,' every one knows, and this hot day draws out our very first yellow rose.
lines.note: You send the first yellow rose in a letter.

lines.text: Pomegranates you may cut deep down the middle and see into, but not hearts,--so why should I try and speak?
lines.note: You use pomegranates and hearts as a guarded metaphor.

lines.text: It is very kind to send these flowers--too kind--why are they sent? and without one single word ... which is not too kind certainly.
lines.note: She questions your flowers sent without a single word.

lines.text: And you are NOT, NOT my 'other friend,' any more than this head of mine is my other head, seeing that I have got a violin which has a head too!
lines.note: You insist she is not merely your other friend.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: You declare love would only grow if she were lost.

lines.text: I was happy, so happy before!
lines.note: You say her gift has made you happier and richer.

lines.text: Dearest, you know how to say what makes me happiest, you who never think, you say, of making me happy!
lines.note: She says you know how to say what makes her happiest.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: She recalls your earlier chestnut-tree west wind.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first direct declaration of love after praising Elizabeth's books.

lines.text: Sympathy is dear--very dear to me: but the sympathy of a poet, and of such a poet, is the quintessence of sympathy to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth answers that a poet's sympathy is the quintessence of sympathy to her.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert looks ahead to spring, friendship, and seeing her at the chapel.

lines.text: This I will say, then--wait and know me better, as you will one long day at the end.
lines.note: Robert asks Elizabeth to know him better over a long day at the end.

lines.text: Well, but, I wanted particularly to say this--Don't bring the 'Duchess' with you on Wednesday.
lines.note: Elizabeth tells Robert not to bring the Duchess, showing their growing ease over his work.

lines.text: Pomegranates you may cut deep down the middle and see into, but not hearts,--so why should I try and speak?
lines.note: Robert's pomegranate image answers Elizabeth's wish to see into things.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's sweeping declaration that his whole life is wound around Elizabeth.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: Elizabeth says Robert is between her and even the closest graves.

lines.text: So I rest on you, for life, for death, beloved--beside you do stand, in my solemn belief, the direct miraculous gift of God to me--that is my solemn belief; may I be thankful!
lines.note: Robert rests his life and death on Elizabeth as God's gift.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: Robert says every word Elizabeth writes goes to his heart and lives there.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's chestnut tree from his earlier letter.

lines.text: And you pretend not to know I would walk barefoot till I dropped, if so I might attain to the sight of you, and it.
lines.note: Robert says he would walk barefoot until he dropped to see Elizabeth.

lines.text: So my dear, own Ba has good sense, best sense—whatever Flush’s may be!
lines.note: Robert marvels that Ba has good sense, best sense.

lines.text: I would not say to you yesterday, perhaps could not, that you wrote ever so much foolishness to me in the morning, dearest, and that I knew it ever so well.
lines.note: Elizabeth says she would not say yesterday's foolishness and knew it well.

lines.text: Do you know I was once not very far from seeing--really seeing you?
lines.note: Your first letter's nearly-seen-you memory opens the whole longing.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Spring promise to see her, echoing that first near-miss.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Her playful answer about spring in her own style, answering your promise.

lines.text: I have but one greater delight in the world than in hearing from you.
lines.note: Later letter where hearing from her is second only to seeing her.

lines.text: I mean such truths as may be painful to me though truths....
lines.note: Her reply that you could write from the end of the world, answering your delight in hearing from her.

lines.text: My only good in this world--that against which all the world goes for nothing--is to spend my life with you, and be yours.
lines.note: Late declaration that your only good is to spend life with her.

lines.text: Let it be this way, ever dearest.
lines.note: Her acceptance of your will as duty and desire.

lines.text: Yet I shall see you on Monday, and shall watch and wait as those who wait for the morning ... that is, the Monday-morning!
lines.note: Her watch-and-wait line for Monday morning.

lines.text: Now, dearest, somehow I can’t write the great proof down—I will tell you on Monday—as to my good sense.
lines.note: Your promise to tell her the proof you cannot write down.

lines.text: Well,—and this is what I meant to say from the beginning of the letter, I love your inability to feel it in spite of right and justice and rationality.
lines.note: Your offer to give back her golden words.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration that he loves her books and her.

lines.text: Mr. Horne never spoke it to my ears--(I never saw him face to face in my life, although we have corresponded for long and long), and he never wrote it to my eyes.
lines.note: He promises that spring will bring their first meeting.

lines.text: You wished all manner of good to me one day as the clock struck ten; yes, and I assure you I was better that day--and I must not forget to tell you so though it is so long since.
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls his clock-striking good wish and its effect on her.

lines.text: Don't you remember I told you, once on a time that you 'knew nothing of me'? whereat you demurred--but I meant what I said, and knew it was so.
lines.note: Robert calls back to his earlier claim that she knew nothing of him.

lines.text: And you are NOT, NOT my 'other friend,' any more than this head of mine is my other head, seeing that I have got a violin which has a head too!
lines.note: A private joke rejecting the idea that she is only his 'other friend'.

lines.text: Do you remember what you said to me of cabbages versus poems, in one of the first letters you ever wrote to me?--of selling cabbages and buying Punches?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls his early cabbage-versus-poem comparison.

lines.text: My own, now!
lines.note: The moment his love becomes openly declared and claimed.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's sweeping image of his life wound around hers.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: His response to her gift of ring and hair, sealing their bond.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: He declares that, if marriage did not exist, he would invent it.

lines.text: Do you remember when you wrote first to me ‘May God bless you and me in that!’
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers his first blessing and how it reached her before they met.

lines.text: And therefore, because you are the best, only dearest!——Robert.
lines.note: Elizabeth finally speaks his name, Robert, as her own.

lines.text: We shall soon know—if you live, you will be mine, I must think—you have put these dear arms too surely round my neck to be disengaged now.
lines.note: Robert's assurance that her life and his are bound together.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letter, asking whether it is her final one.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert’s first open declaration of love, setting the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: Is it indeed true that I was so near to the pleasure and honour of making your acquaintance? and can it be true that you look back upon the lost opportunity with any regret?
lines.note: Elizabeth answers his story of nearly seeing her, turning a missed meeting into intimate possibility.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert’s spring promise to see her, a recurring seasonal hope in their letters.

lines.text: I shall be ready on Tuesday I hope, but I hate and protest against your horrible 'entomology.'
lines.note: Elizabeth fixes the first visit while joking about his ‘entomology,’ a private shorthand from their early meetings.

lines.text: I do believe we are friends now and for ever.
lines.note: After the first meetings, Robert names their bond as friendship ‘now and for ever.’

lines.text: Yes, I admit that it was stupid to read that word so wrong.
lines.note: Elizabeth confesses misreading a word, one of their small shared corrections and private jokes.

lines.text: Think for me, speak for me, my dearest, my own!
lines.note: Robert asks Elizabeth to think and speak for him as their love becomes explicit.

lines.text: Then first, ... first, I ask you not to misunderstand.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks him not to misunderstand her first request, marking a careful turn in their courtship.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: Robert’s response to Elizabeth’s gift of hair and the ring, carrying their private symbolism.

lines.text: I will care for it no more, dearest--I am wedded to you now.
lines.note: Robert declares himself ‘wedded’ to her, a decisive private vow before marriage.

lines.text: And therefore, because you are the best, only dearest!——Robert.
lines.note: Elizabeth finally speaks Robert’s name, turning a long-deferred intimacy into tenderness.

lines.text: We must be married directly and go to Italy.
lines.note: The urgent decision to marry and leave for Italy before separation can intervene.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s final letter before they depart together, full of love and farewell to the old life.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Opening declaration that his letter is not mere compliment; it establishes the book-love that starts everything.

lines.text: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart.
lines.note: Her first reply, thanking him from the bottom of her heart and naming a poet's sympathy the quintessence.

lines.text: Only don't let us have any constraint, any ceremony!
lines.note: Her early plea against ceremony and for honest speech; it sets the friendship's tone.

lines.text: I have believed in your skulls for the last year, for my part.
lines.note: Private joke about believing in his skulls, showing the playful intimacy already established.

lines.text: I do believe we are friends now and for ever.
lines.note: He declares their friendship fixed now and for ever, marking the turn from acquaintances to friends.

lines.text: You let 'flowers be sent you in a letter,' every one knows, and this hot day draws out our very first yellow rose.
lines.note: She recalls his yellow rose in a letter and its omen, a callback to their first exchanged flowers.

lines.text: And you do like the 'Duchess,' as much as you have got of it? that delights me, too--for every reason.
lines.note: She asks if he likes the 'Duchess', showing her close reading and growing investment in his work.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: His Shrove-Tuesday fowl joke is a private, unmistakably theirs moment of teasing.

lines.text: Even at the risk of teazing you a little I must say a few words, that there may be no misunderstanding between us--and this, before I sleep to-night.
lines.note: She insists on no misunderstanding before sleep, a tense turn about their future and boundaries.

lines.text: There is nothing in you that does not draw out all of me.
lines.note: He says nothing in her fails to draw out all of him, the clearest early avowal.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: He says his whole life is wound round her, an intimate declaration.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: He says every word she writes lives in his heart, deepening the bond.

lines.text: When you are gone I find your flowers; and you never spoke of nor showed them to me--so instead of yesterday I thank you to-day--thank you.
lines.note: She thanks him for flowers he never mentioned, a tender callback to his secret kindness.

lines.text: Ah, love,--you are my unutterable blessing,--I discover you, more of you, day by day,--hour by hour, I do think!--I am entirely yours,--one gratitude, all my soul becomes when I see you over me as now--God bless my dear, dearest.
lines.note: He calls her his unutterable blessing, a culminating love note.

lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first direct declaration of love, establishing the emotional core.

lines.text: This is in my heart to say to you--and I say it.
lines.note: Elizabeth's private, heartfelt admission that something is in her heart to say.

lines.text: I had been thinking so of seeing you on Tuesday ... with my sister's eyes--for the first sight.
lines.note: Elizabeth's tender anticipation of seeing Robert for the first time.

lines.text: I am proud and happy in your friendship--now and ever.
lines.note: Robert's firm statement of pride and happiness in Elizabeth's friendship.

lines.text: Dearest, I will end here--words, persuasion, arguments, if they were at my service I would not use them--I believe in you, altogether have faith in you--in you.
lines.note: Robert's pivotal avowal that his love and faith are placed entirely in Elizabeth.

lines.text: But that God is stronger than we, cannot be a bitter thought to you but a holy thought ... while He lets me, as much as I can be anyone's, be only yours.
lines.note: Elizabeth's trusting response that God's strength is greater than their fears.

lines.text: I write one word just to say that it is all over with Pisa; which was a probable evil when I wrote last, and which I foresaw from the beginning--being a prophetess, you know.
lines.note: Elizabeth's quiet announcement that Pisa is lost and she yields to necessity.

lines.text: Words can never tell you, however,—form them, transform them anyway,—how perfectly dear you are to me—perfectly dear to my heart and soul.
lines.note: Robert's retrospective gratitude for every word and gesture of their courtship.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: Elizabeth's brief, overwhelmed word that the day feels like a dream.

lines.text: It seems all like a dream!
lines.note: Elizabeth's awe that their secret marriage seems like a dream.

lines.text: And for the rest, if either of us two is to suffer injury and sorrow for what happened there to-day—I pray that it may all fall upon me!
lines.note: Elizabeth's prayer that any injury from the marriage fall on her rather than Robert.

lines.text: My own beloved, if ever you should have reason to complain of me in things voluntary and possible, all other women would have a right to tread me underfoot, I should be so vile and utterly unworthy.
lines.note: Elizabeth's gentle reassurance that she can now openly love Robert.

lines.text: Real warm Spring, dear Miss Barrett, and the birds know it; and in Spring I shall see you, surely see you--for when did I once fail to get whatever I had set my heart upon?
lines.note: Robert's early promise of spring and seeing Elizabeth anchors the poem's longing.

lines.text: Some things you say are very touching, and some, surprising; and although I am aware that you unconsciously exaggerate what I can be to you, yet it is delightful to be broad awake and think of you as my friend.
lines.note: Elizabeth's delight in being thought of as a friend gives the missing-you feeling warmth.

lines.text: You let 'flowers be sent you in a letter,' every one knows, and this hot day draws out our very first yellow rose.
lines.note: Robert's yellow rose sent in a letter is a concrete token of care.

lines.text: So, till to-morrow,--my light through the dark week.
lines.note: Robert calls Elizabeth his light through the dark week.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: Elizabeth's vivid Shrove-Tuesday image captures their playful, intimate bond.

lines.text: Do you know, dear friend, it is no good policy to stop up all the vents of my feeling, nor leave one for safety's sake, as you will do, let me caution you never so repeatedly.
lines.note: Robert's caution about shutting up all feeling suits the ache of absence.

lines.text: But your 'Saul' is unobjectionable as far as I can see, my dear friend.
lines.note: Elizabeth's praise of Robert's poem shows how closely she follows his work.

lines.text: Only a word to tell you Moxon promises the books for to-morrow, Wednesday--so towards evening yours will reach you--'parve liber, sine me ibis' ... would I were by you, then and ever!
lines.note: Robert wishes he were by Elizabeth when sending his book.

lines.text: I had your note last night, and am waiting for the book to-day; a true living breathing book, let the writer say of it what he will.
lines.note: Elizabeth's comfort that the book will not come 'sine te' mirrors the same longing.

lines.text: I was happy, so happy before!
lines.note: Robert's happiness in Elizabeth's gift conveys how much her presence means.

lines.text: You will only expect a few words—what will those be?
lines.note: Robert's full heart and the wish to do better for Elizabeth close the story with devotion.

lines.text: My own beloved, if ever you should have reason to complain of me in things voluntary and possible, all other women would have a right to tread me underfoot, I should be so vile and utterly unworthy.
lines.note: Elizabeth's gratitude for being lifted into life and sunshine answers his longing.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Robert's waking well and thanking Elizabeth's gift ends on hope and love.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Opening declaration that your verses and you are loved; sets the whole correspondence in motion.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Early promise to wait for friendship and spring, before the first meeting.

lines.text: In art, however, I understand that it does not do to be headlong, but patient and laborious--and there is a love strong enough, even in me, to overcome nature.
lines.note: Elizabeth's reply that love can overcome nature, echoing the growing bond.

lines.text: Yes, but, dear Mr. Browning, I want the spring according to the new 'style' (mine), and not the old one of you and the rest of the poets.
lines.note: Playful disagreement about spring, showing her own voice and wit.

lines.text: You tie me like a Shrove-Tuesday fowl to a stake and then pick the thickest cudgel out of your lot, and at my head it goes--I wonder whether you remembered having predicted exactly the same horror once before.
lines.note: Playful, vivid image of being tied and cudgelled; their banter at its sharpest.

lines.text: But I never did strike you or touch you--and you are not in earnest in the complaint you make--and this is really all I am going to say to-day.
lines.note: Her answer that she never struck you, turning the same playful quarrel back.

lines.text: And now--here I refuse to fancy--you KNOW whether, if you never write another line, speak another intelligible word, recognize me by a look again--whether I shall love you less or more ...
lines.note: Love declared as total and unwavering, in the autumn of 1845.

lines.text: How you overcome me as always you do--and where is the answer to anything except too deep down in the heart for even the pearl-divers?
lines.note: Her response that your love overcomes her and leaves no answer.

lines.text: Take it, dearest; what I am forced to think you mean--and take no more with it--for I gave all to give long ago--I am all yours--and now, mine; give me mine to be happy with!
lines.note: The ring moment: asking her to take what you mean and be yours.

lines.text: It comes at eight o'clock--the post says eight ...
lines.note: Her answer about the ring arriving, with its purple lock and hair.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Callback to your chestnut-tree line from the first year, now turned back to you.

lines.text: No, my own dearest, I did not see you sit in your chair, nor in mine, yesterday—did I write nothing about your walking with me by the garden wall, and on the hill, and looking down on London?
lines.note: After the secret marriage, reassuring that you did not see her in the chair.

lines.text: Dearest and ever dearest, try to forgive me when I fall so manifestly short of you in all things!
lines.note: Late letter of gratitude and hope, near the end of the preserved correspondence.

lines.text: Did you really kiss me on the two eyes, my Ba?
lines.note: Her final question whether you really kissed her, closing with tenderness.

lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's first letter openly declares love for Elizabeth's verses and for her, establishing the courtship.

lines.text: I feel that if I could get myself remade, as if turned to gold, I WOULD not even then desire to become more than the mere setting to that diamond you must always wear.
lines.note: Robert tells Elizabeth she is the diamond and he only the setting, a vivid image of devotion.

lines.text: The tear-marks went away in the moisture of new, happy tears.
lines.note: Elizabeth's tear-marks turning into happy tears shows the emotional turn of their relationship.

lines.text: When I wrote that letter to let you come the first time, do you know, the tears ran down my cheeks....
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls crying when she first allowed Robert to visit, marking how much that first meeting mattered.

lines.text: And now I will dare ... yes, dearest, kiss you back to my heart again; my own.
lines.note: Robert's intimate closing line captures their deepening physical and emotional closeness.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: Robert's playful declaration that he would invent marriage if it did not exist signals their commitment.

lines.text: My only good in this world--that against which all the world goes for nothing--is to spend my life with you, and be yours.
lines.note: Robert frames his whole good in life as spending it with Elizabeth, anchoring the marriage plan.

lines.text: Can it be the same 'Luria,' I think, that 'golden-hearted Luria,' whom you talked of to me, when you complained of keeping 'wild company,' in the old dear letter?
lines.note: Elizabeth connects the printed 'Luria' back to Robert's earlier 'golden-hearted Luria,' a callback to their literary courtship.

lines.text: ‘know I now what love is!’—Do you remember that the first word I ever wrote to you was ‘I love you, dear Miss Barrett?’
lines.note: Robert recalls that his first written words to Elizabeth were love, echoing the opening of their correspondence.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's final note imagines having Robert alone to love, closing the poem on their imminent union.

lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: An early sign of their secret understanding and engagement.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: Elizabeth's beloved Flush welcomes her home, a private domestic image.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert's affectionate close to one of the earliest letters.

lines.text: Here is a distress for me, dearest!
lines.note: The crisis of Flush being stolen, an ordeal they share.

lines.text: Poor Flush—how sorry I am for you, my Ba!
lines.note: Robert's sympathy for Elizabeth after Flush's theft.

lines.text: Dearest, you are a prophet, I suppose—there can be no denying it.
lines.note: Elizabeth's family is suddenly ordered away, forcing their plans.

lines.text: You will only expect a few words—what will those be?
lines.note: Robert's reflection on their wedding day.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: Elizabeth's account of the strain and relief of the wedding day.

lines.text: I feel so as if I had slipped down over the wall into somebody’s garden—I feel ashamed.
lines.note: Elizabeth's dizzy sense of having slipped into a new life.

lines.text: You take my words from me—I ‘exult’ in the irrevocability of this precious bestowal of yourself on me—come what will my life has borne flower and fruit—it is a glorious, successful, felicitous life, I thank God and you.
lines.note: Robert's exultation at their marriage.

lines.text: First, God is to be thanked for this great joy of hearing that you are better, my ever dearest—it is a joy that floats over all the other emotions.
lines.note: Elizabeth's gratitude and anxiety about her father after the marriage.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Her last letter before they leave together for Italy.

lines.note: Opening recognition between them, setting the private understanding of their early exchange. Callbacks: []

lines.note: Robert’s affectionate, intimate turn of phrase, a vivid early moment of closeness. Callbacks: []

lines.text: I have just come from the vestry of Paddington chapel, and bore it very well, and saw nobody except one woman.
lines.note: Elizabeth reports a small, practical victory over her fear of crowds, showing her growing steadiness. Callbacks: []

lines.text: Here is dearest Ba’s dearest letter, because the latest, and it is one of her very kisses incorporated and made manifest—so perfectly kind!
lines.note: Robert responds to her love with grateful wonder, marking a deepening emotional exchange. Callbacks: []

lines.note: Early moment where she assures him she already understood him.

lines.text: If I did not love you, how I would begin now!
lines.note: His direct avowal that love would begin even if it had not already.

lines.text: How I wish for two hearts to love you with, and two lives to give to you, and two souls to bear the weight worthily of all you have given to me.
lines.note: Her wish for two hearts and lives to give him.

lines.text: No indeed—I think I should never be afraid, if you were near enough.
lines.note: Her confidence that she would not be afraid with him near.

lines.text: I have just come from the vestry of Paddington chapel, and bore it very well, and saw nobody except one woman.
lines.note: She returns to the chapel and bears it well.

lines.text: Only a few words to tell you that Flush is found, and lying on the sofa, with one paw and both ears hanging over the edge of it.
lines.note: Flush is found and lying on the sofa again.

lines.text: How I shall need your letters, dearest!
lines.note: He says he will need her letters while apart.

lines.text: The sight of your letter, even, did not provoke the cloud—that was only the lesser joy, I thought, preceding the greater!
lines.note: She receives his letter and then faces sudden sadness.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: After the marriage she writes that all is safe so far.

lines.text: Bless you, my very own, only Ba—my pride, and joy, and utter comfort.
lines.note: His closing gratitude, pride, and comfort in her.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Her final eve-of-departure word before they leave together.

lines.text: And something I said in my letter, which was wrong to say and I am sorry to think of—forgive me that, ever beloved—but you have forgiven, I know.
lines.note: Elizabeth admits she said something wrong and asks Robert to forgive her, matching the sorry occasion.

lines.text: Will you come, dearest, after all?
lines.note: Elizabeth asks whether Robert will come after all, capturing the anxious middle of their separation.

lines.text: I will say no more, praying you to forgive whatever you shall judge to need forgiveness here,—dearest Ba!
lines.note: Robert prays that Elizabeth forgive whatever needs forgiveness, a direct apology in the correspondence.

lines.text: Will you not forgive me a word so spoken, Robert? will you rather set it against me as if habitually I threw to you levities in change for earnest devotion?—you imply that of me.
lines.note: Elizabeth asks Robert to forgive a lightly spoken word, continuing their apology-and-forgiveness thread.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: Elizabeth writes that she has lost Flush, a sharp emotional turn that only they would recognise.

lines.text: Will you be tolerant, my Ba, and forgive me—till to-morrow at least—when, what with physic, what with impatience, I shall be better one way or another?
lines.note: Robert asks Elizabeth to be tolerant and forgive him until he is better, another direct apology.

lines.note: Elizabeth reports that Flush is found and lying on the sofa, resolving the earlier loss.

lines.text: How I miss you, and long for Friday.
lines.note: A direct expression of missing Robert before a planned meeting.

lines.note: A small concrete victory over crowds and nerves on a Sunday.

lines.note: The saga's comic resolution, with Flush sprawled on the sofa.

lines.text: Will you, among the other kisses, give him one for me?
lines.note: Robert asks for a proxy kiss for Flush, continuing the private joke.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: A turning point where Elizabeth commits to Robert's decision.

lines.text: Do you pray for me to-night, Robert?
lines.note: A final intimate appeal to Robert on the last night before leaving.

lines.note: Elizabeth opens with their private shorthand of understanding.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert admits he sometimes shortened visits just to reach the moment of taking her hand.

lines.text: How I wish for two hearts to love you with, and two lives to give to you, and two souls to bear the weight worthily of all you have given to me.
lines.note: Elizabeth's wish for two hearts and two lives is one of the letter's most intimate declarations.

lines.text: Is this absence contrived on purpose to prove how foolishly I said that I loved you the more from seeing you the oftener?
lines.note: Robert teases that absence seems designed to test his claim about loving her more.

lines.text: Chiappino little knew how right he was, when he used to taunt me with my ‘New Cross Knight.’
lines.note: Elizabeth revives the private 'New Cross Knight' taunt from Chiappino.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: The sudden loss of Flush brings one of the correspondence's most vivid domestic alarms.

lines.text: ‘Our friend and follower, that was to be’—is that, then, your opinion of my poor darling Flush’s destiny— Ah,—I should not have been so quiet if I had not known differently and better.
lines.note: Elizabeth answers Robert's 'friend and follower' phrase after Flush's rescue.

lines.text: ‘The milk,’ answers Ba, is exactly to correct the superabundant gall of bitterness which overflowed lately about Flush.
lines.note: Robert turns the milk-diet into a witty callback during the Flush dispute.

lines.text: And smiling to myself I was, both last night and this morning, at your phrase about the ‘business’ to be talked by the ‘grave man and woman’; understanding your precaution against all unlawful jesting!—jesters forbidden in the protocol!
lines.note: Elizabeth jokes that jesters are forbidden by their 'protocol,' echoing their grave-business talk.

lines.text: You have given me the highest, completest proof of love that ever one human being gave another.
lines.note: Robert calls her gift of herself the highest proof of love one person can give another.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: Elizabeth's 'oh, such a day!' captures the breathless aftermath of the wedding.

lines.text: Dearest, dearestest!—And you do not start at that word, ‘Irrevocable,’ as I have had fancies that you might, when the time came!’
lines.note: Elizabeth tests whether Robert will flinch at the word 'Irrevocable.'

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Her question about this being her last letter gives the farewell its final ache.

lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Opens with the intimate understanding that defines their letters.

lines.note: Concrete, joyful image of Flush’s reunion, a private household moment.

lines.text: Now I will kiss you, dearest: used you to divine that at the very beginning, I have sometimes shortened the visit in order to arrive at the time of taking your hand?
lines.note: Robert’s tender habit of shortening visits to reach her hand.

lines.note: Elizabeth’s passionate wish to give him two hearts and lives.

lines.text: When birds have their eyes out, they are apt to be mumpish.
lines.note: A vivid private joke about her father calling her mumpish.

lines.text: I think only that you love me, that you are the angel of my life,—and for the despair and desolation behind me, they serve to mark the hour of your coming,—and they are behind, as Italy is before.
lines.note: Her declaration that he is the angel of her life.

lines.text: I shall live for you, for every minute in your life.
lines.note: Robert’s promise to live for her every minute.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: The sudden loss of Flush, one of their most shared anxieties.

lines.note: Elizabeth’s affectionate rebuttal about Flush’s destiny.

lines.text: I am rejoiced that poor Flush is found again, dearest—altogether rejoiced.
lines.note: Robert’s relief and rejoicing at Flush’s return.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: Their playful comparison: she is his Flush, and he is hers.

lines.text: What could be better than lifting me from the ground and carrying me into life and the sunshine?

lines.note: Elizabeth’s promise to keep that bud for life.

lines.text: I thought once that the capacity of happiness was destroyed in me, but you have made it over again,—God has permitted you!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s happiness is remade by him after long despair.

lines.text: Our adventure, indeed!
lines.note: Their shared word for the life-changing step they are taking.

lines.note: Robert’s homely apple parable about not delaying their happiness.

lines.note: Her affectionate command that he come back safe, even without Flush.

lines.text: And smiling to myself I was, both last night and this morning, at your phrase about the ‘business’ to be talked by the ‘grave man and woman’; understanding your precaution against all unlawful jesting!—jesters forbidden in the protocol!
lines.note: Elizabeth smiles at Robert’s grave ‘business’ talk while jesters are forbidden.

lines.text: For Flush, I did your commission, kissing the top of his head: then I took the kiss back again because it seemed too good for him just now.
lines.note: Flush becomes a playful go-between for their kisses.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: The exhausted, breathless morning after the wedding.

lines.text: And forgive the inveterate jesting, which jests with eyes full of tears.
lines.note: Jesting through tears at the edge of their new life.

lines.note: Her last letter before they leave England together.

lines.note: Your promise that now you possess her, you renew the offer to possess you, sealing the new relation.

lines.text: And then ... imagine the comfort I take to the deepest of my heart from these hands held out to me!
lines.note: Her comfort in the hands held out to her by your family, a grateful acceptance of your world.

lines.text: If you do go on Monday, our marriage will be impossible for another year—the misery!
lines.note: Robert's urgency about marriage shows the elopement's stakes.

lines.text: Dearest, I write one word, and have one will which is yours.
lines.note: Elizabeth's surrender of will marks the decisive turning point.

lines.text: Words can never tell you, however,—form them, transform them anyway,—how perfectly dear you are to me—perfectly dear to my heart and soul.
lines.note: Robert's retrospective praise crowns their early correspondence.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
lines.note: Elizabeth's first post-wedding letter carries relief and dreamlike disorientation.

lines.text: I feel so as if I had slipped down over the wall into somebody’s garden—I feel ashamed.
lines.note: Elizabeth's garden-wall image captures her post-marriage wonder.

lines.text: Thank you a thousand times for the note, my own Ba.
lines.note: Robert's gratitude answers her wedding-day proof of love.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: The final eve before departure distills everything to 'you only'.

lines.text: Your letters to me I take with me, let the ‘ounces’ cry out aloud, ever so.
lines.note: She cannot leave his letters behind, sealing the archive of their courtship.

lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Early, private shorthand: Elizabeth says she understood his words better than he thought.

lines.text: When I opened my door on my return, Flush threw himself upon me with a most ecstatical agony, and for full ten minutes did not cease jumping and kissing my hands—he thought he had lost me for certain, this time.
lines.note: A vivid domestic moment: Flush’s ecstatic reunion with Elizabeth.

lines.text: Friday will come however,—and I may as well go on to tell you that Mrs. Jameson came yesterday.
lines.note: Mrs Jameson arrives asking ‘Anything settled?’, showing how close their secret is to exposure.

lines.text: The cushion of the armchair!
lines.note: A tiny, odd exclamation that feels like a private joke between them.

lines.text: Here is the bad news going to you as fast as bad news will go! for you ‘do really (NOT) see me to-morrow,’ Robert,—there is no chance of it for such ‘too, two’ wise people as we are!
lines.note: Elizabeth reverses the expected meeting with abrupt bad news.

lines.text: I was beginning to dress, hours before the proper time, through the confidence of seeing you now,—after the letter which came early in the morning,—when this new letter changes everything.
lines.note: Robert caught dressing hours early, then undone by her changed letter.

lines.text: Here is a distress for me, dearest!
lines.note: Flush is stolen, a major turn in the story.

lines.text: I am sure you are grieved and frightened for our friend and follower, that was to be, at Pisa—will you not write a special note to tell me when you get him again?
lines.note: Robert calls Flush ‘our friend and follower, that was to be.’

lines.text: ‘Our friend and follower, that was to be’—is that, then, your opinion of my poor darling Flush’s destiny— Ah,—I should not have been so quiet if I had not known differently and better.
lines.note: Elizabeth quotes Robert’s ‘friend and follower’ phrase back to him.

lines.text: Was ever any in the world, in any possible world, so perfectly good and dear to another as you are to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth’s sweeping, specific praise of Robert’s goodness.

lines.text: You will only expect a few words—what will those be?
lines.note: Robert’s full-heart note after the wedding day.

lines.text: Ever dearest, I write a word that you may read it and know how all is safe so far, and that I am not slain downright with the day—oh, such a day!
